grammar.explanation: A Korean sentence ends with its predicate: a verb, an adjective, or 이다. The subject usually comes first and any object sits between the subject and the verb, so "I eat an apple" becomes "I apple eat". Particles attached to each noun show what role it plays.

Attach 는 to a noun ending in a vowel and 은 to one ending in a consonant. It marks the topic of the sentence, which at this stage is usually the subject. 저 (formal) and 나 (informal) both mean "I", giving 저는 and 나는.
Attach 를 after a vowel and 을 after a consonant to mark the object, the thing the verb acts on. The object goes before the verb at the end of the sentence.

이다 links two nouns to say that A is B, and it attaches directly to the second noun. In polite speech it becomes 이에요 after a consonant and 예요 after a vowel. It is not used with adjectives, because Korean adjectives already include the meaning "to be".

이 points to something near the speaker, 그 to something near the listener or already mentioned, and 저 to something far from both. They go in front of a noun (이 사람, 저 나무). Combined with 것 (thing) they become the pronouns 이것, 그것 and 저것.

examples.en: That over there is a tree.
That person over there is a doctor.

grammar.explanation: Attach 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel to mark the grammatical subject. When 이/가 attaches to 저 or 나, they change to 제가 and 내가. Unlike 는/은, which sets up a topic, 이/가 simply points to who or what does or is something.

examples.en: The cat is in the room.
The book is on the table.

grammar.explanation: To say someone has something, use "Person는/은 Thing이/가 있다". The thing owned takes 이/가, not 을/를, because 있다 here works like "Thing exists for the person".
~에 attaches to a place or a time. With 있다 it shows where something is. With movement verbs like 가다 it shows where someone is going, and with time words it means "at" or "on".

examples.en: The milk is in the fridge.
The cat is in the room.

grammar.explanation: To describe position, put the reference noun first and then a position noun such as 안, 위, 밑, 옆, 뒤 or 앞, followed by ~에 있다. "On the table" becomes "table top-at" (탁자 위에).

examples.en: The pen is on the table.
The dog is under the chair.
The bank is next to the hotel.
The restaurant is in front of the school.

grammar.point: Verbs: dictionary form ~다 and the stem
grammar.explanation: Every Korean verb ends in 다 in its dictionary form. Removing 다 leaves the stem, and endings for tense and politeness attach to it. The verb goes at the end of the sentence and can take an object marked with 을/를.

Korean adjectives also end in 다 and are conjugated like verbs. They already contain the idea of "to be", so 크다 means "to be big" and no 이다 is needed. They describe the subject and never take an object.
Put 의 between two nouns to make the first one the owner: "A의 B" means "A's B". 저의 and 나의 are often shortened to 제 and 내. In speech 의 is frequently dropped when the meaning is clear.
좋다 is an adjective meaning "to be good", so it describes the subject and takes no object. 좋아하다 is a verb meaning "to like" and takes an object marked with 을/를.
우리 means "we" or "us", and before a noun it means "our". Koreans often say 우리 where English uses "my" for shared things like a home, a family member or a country.

To place an adjective before a noun, add ㄴ to a stem ending in a vowel (크다 → 큰) and 은 to a stem ending in a consonant (작다 → 작은). A stem ending in ㄹ drops the ㄹ and takes ㄴ (길다 → 긴). Adjectives ending in 있다 take 는 instead (맛있는, 재미있는).

examples.en: The happy woman lives in a small house.
That man is a fun person.

grammar.point: 많다 (to be many): 많은 + noun vs noun이/가 많다
grammar.explanation: 많다 can describe a noun as 많은 ("a lot of") or act as the predicate in "Noun이/가 많다" ("there are many of the noun"). The predicate pattern is the more natural way to say that a place has a lot of something.

examples.en: There are many people on the street.
I have a lot of money.
I eat a lot of food.

grammar.explanation: ~도 means "also" and replaces 는/은, 이/가 or 을/를 on the noun. Its meaning depends on which noun it attaches to: 저도 means "I also (do it)", while 사과도 means "(I eat) apples too".

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Korean Conjugation: Past, Present, Future

grammar.explanation: In the plain written style, a verb stem ending in a vowel takes ~ㄴ다 (가다 → 간다) and a stem ending in a consonant takes ~는다 (먹다 → 먹는다). Adjectives stay in their basic 다 form in the present tense.
If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았다. Otherwise add 었다, and 하 becomes 했다. When the stem ends in a vowel the two usually merge (가았다 → 갔다, 배우었다 → 배웠다, 던지었다 → 던졌다).

examples.en: I went to the store yesterday.
My younger sibling threw the ball.

grammar.explanation: Add ~겠다 to any stem, whether it ends in a vowel or a consonant, to express what you will do. It works most naturally for the speaker's own intentions.

examples.en: I will go to the museum.
We will leave the day after tomorrow.
I will read a book today.

grammar.explanation: 저 is the formal "I" and 나 the informal one, becoming 제가 and 내가 with 이/가. Koreans usually avoid a direct word for "you". They use the person's title or a family term instead, use 너 only with close friends or younger people (너 + 가 becomes 네가), and rarely use 당신.

examples.en: Are you (teacher) going to school today?

grammar.explanation: Add 아 to a stem whose last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and 어 otherwise, and 하 becomes 해. This casual form is used with close friends, younger people or children. The past tense is ~았어/었어 and the future is ~겠어.

examples.en: My younger sibling is sleeping now.

grammar.explanation: Add 요 to the informal low form to make it polite. This is the most common everyday polite speech, used with strangers, coworkers and older people. Past is ~았어요/었어요 and future is ~겠어요.

examples.en: I am waiting for my friend.

grammar.explanation: Add ㅂ니다 to a stem ending in a vowel and 습니다 to one ending in a consonant. For past and future, add 습니다 after 았/었 or 겠. This form is used in formal settings such as news, speeches, the military or talking to a boss.

examples.en: I am waiting for the boss.
The students sit in the classroom.

vocab.en: to be hard, to be rigid

grammar.explanation: Some stems ending in ㅅ, such as 짓다, lose the ㅅ when the next ending starts with a vowel: 짓 + 어요 → 지어요. Not every ㅅ stem does this (웃다 → 웃어요 is regular), so these verbs have to be memorized.

examples.en: That company built a big building.

grammar.explanation: In some stems ending in ㄷ, such as 듣다 and 걷다, the ㄷ changes to ㄹ before an ending that starts with a vowel: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸었어요. Others, like 닫다 and 받다, stay regular.
Most adjectives whose stem ends in ㅂ change the ㅂ to 우 before a vowel ending, and the 우 then merges with 어: 춥다 → 추워요, 쉽다 → 쉬워요. 돕다 is an exception that becomes 도와요.
When a stem ends in the vowel ㅡ, the ㅡ disappears before 아/어. Use 아 if the vowel before it is ㅏ or ㅗ and 어 otherwise: 바쁘다 → 바빠요, 예쁘다 → 예뻐요, 쓰다 → 써요.
When a stem ends in 르 and is followed by 아/어, the ㅡ drops and an extra ㄹ is added, giving ㄹ라 or ㄹ러: 다르다 → 달라요, 빠르다 → 빨라요, 모르다 → 몰라요.

examples.en: I don't know that person's name.

grammar.explanation: A stem ending in ㄹ drops the ㄹ when the next part starts with ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ: 살다 → 삽니다, 알다 → 압니다, 길다 → 긴. Before an ending that starts with a vowel the ㄹ stays (살아요).

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Korean Adverbs, Negative Sentences in Korean

vocab.en: to be sick, to be sore

grammar.point: Adverbs of time, place and degree
grammar.explanation: Adverbs describe when, where or how much something happens. Time and place words usually come near the start of the sentence. Degree and frequency adverbs like 자주, 빨리 and 많이 go right before the verb they modify.

examples.en: I often go to the library.

grammar.explanation: Many adverbs are made by adding ~게 to an adjective stem (쉽다 → 쉽게). Adjectives ending in 하다 can often swap 하다 for 히 as well (안전하게 or 안전히). A few have special forms, such as 많다 → 많이 and 빠르다 → 빨리.
Put 안 directly before the final verb or adjective to make it negative. For noun + 하다 verbs such as 공부하다, 안 goes between the noun and 하다 (공부 안 하다).

examples.en: My younger sibling doesn't go to school.

grammar.explanation: Add ~지 않다 to the stem of the final verb or adjective, then conjugate 않다 for tense and politeness. It means the same as 안 but sounds a little more formal or written.

examples.en: I won't go to school tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: 아니다 is the negative of 이다. The noun before it takes 이/가: "A는 B이/가 아니다" means "A is not B". The polite form is 아니에요.

examples.en: That person is not a foreigner.

grammar.point: 없다 (to not have / not be there)
grammar.explanation: 없다 is the opposite of 있다. "Person는 Thing이/가 없다" means the person does not have it, and "Thing이/가 Place에 없다" means it is not at that place.

examples.en: My friend isn't at the library now.
There are no drinks in the fridge.

grammar.explanation: This pair works like 좋아하다 and 좋다. 싫어하다 is a verb meaning "to dislike" and takes an object with 을/를. 싫다 is an adjective, so the disliked thing is marked with 이/가 and becomes the subject.
